rationale:
Evidence: iteration 9 is the best design so far (697.2). It is iteration 6 with the sensors moved forward from y 0.06 to 0.07. Oval finished 20/20 (1.96 s), s-bend finished 20/20 and was faster than iteration 6 (2.33 s vs 2.42 s), and slalom progress rose slightly (0.494 vs 0.474). Forward look-ahead therefore helped marginally with no completion loss. Slalom remains 0/20: it leaves the line in about 19 of 20 runs at roughly half the course, with about 1.3 line-loss events per run. Iteration 7 (kp 5, kd 1.0) and iteration 8 (16 mm sensors, +/-4 cm) both lost s-bend finishes, so the controller gain and the wide-footprint sensing are both near their limits.

Changes (small, one-variable step): sensors moved forward again from y 0.07 to 0.075, the largest step that stays well inside the allowed y range and keeps the sensor footprints clear of the axle. Geometry otherwise matches iteration 9 (12 mm footprints, +/-3 cm, 1 cm spacing, seven sensors). Controller is identical to iteration 9 (base 1.3, kp 4.8, ki 0.5, kd 0.9, same weights, last_direction), so the score change can be attributed to the look-ahead alone.

Expected result: slalom progress rises modestly, toward 0.5 to 0.55, with a small chance of a first slalom completion; oval and s-bend hold at 20/20. Risk: more look-ahead adds phase lead at low speed, which could raise s-bend max_error. Hypotheses: (a) additional look-ahead reduces slalom line losses (target about 1.0 per run or fewer); (b) if s-bend finishes drop below 18/20 or max_error exceeds 0.02 on s-bend, the forward shift has passed its useful point and y should return to 0.07. Measurements wanted: completion and completion_time by track; progress, max_error and line_loss_events on slalom (location of the line loss); s-bend finish count and steering_oscillation (to check lag).
